newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia yr-on-yr April CPI up mild 2.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia yr-on-yr April CPI up mild 2.6 pct.

text.p: Malaysia's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by a mild 2.6 percent year-on-year in April, the smallest increase in years, economists said on Friday.
The measure of inflation at the retail level was led by a 0.7 percent decline in clothing and footwear prices, the Statistics Department said in a report.

Consumer prices have typically hovered in a three percent to four percent band over the past few years. Bank Negara Malaysia, the country's central bank, has had a policy for the past several years of keeping inflation under four percent.
But economists said they could scarcely remember the last time the index had showed less than three percent growth.
"I think it's been holding above three percent for quite some time so the 2.6 percent number is a bit surprising," said Kevin Chew, an economist with Caspian Securities.

He said sweeping reductions in import duties announced in the previous two national budgets had had an "accruing effect on economy". The government's efforts at price and other administrative controls had contributed as well, he said.
Kostas Panagiotou, senior economist at Kim Eng Securities, said: "I would think people were expecting around three percent. Normally, the market does not react, but this is quite a big drop."
The stock market showed little immediate reaction to the inflation news, posting a 13.46 point drop, or 1.29 percent, to 1,027.81 at the midday break on Friday.
Currency markets were also unmoved by the CPI report, with the ringgit focused on its own factors. The Malaysian unit recovered on Friday as offshore players unwound long dollar positions.
At 0527 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.4810/30 to the dollar after being quoted at 2.4900/20 at 0300 GMT.
In other component breakdowns, the April CPI recorded year-on-year 0.1 percent gains each in costs for furniture as well as in cultural services, which include recreation and entertainment.

Year-on-year, food showed the biggest price increase of the eight main components, with a 4.3 percent gain. That was followed by a 3.5 percent rise in medical care and health expenses and three percent cost gains in rent, fuel and power.
Compared with March, the CPI eased by 0.2 percent, as food prices fell 0.6 percent and clothing and footwear declined 0.2 percent, the department said.
